source: Hand-converted from the CBSE Class X 2025-26 sample-paper marking schemes in public/papers/ (class10-science-2025-26-ms.pdf, class10-mathematics-basic-2025-26-ms.pdf, class10-social-science-2025-26-ms.pdf). Every rubric is a draft for a teacher to review; see data/rubrics.schema.md.

rubrics.subject: Science
rubrics.prompt: Unlike animals, plants do not have any excretory products as they do not eat food. Comment upon the statement with justification.

scheme.excerpt: It is completely wrong to say that plants do not produce any excretory products. However, plants use completely different strategies for excretion than those of the animals. They get rid of these wastes in different manner (any two): i. Oxygen, a photosynthetic waste, is removed through stomata. ii. Excess water is removed by transpiration through stomata. iii. Other metabolic wastes are either stored in dead cells, resins and gums or are removed through falling of old leaves. iv. Many waste products are stored in cellular vacuoles [2]

steps.awardFor: any two strategies plants use to get rid of waste

options.awardFor: oxygen, a photosynthetic waste, is removed through stomata
excess water is removed by transpiration
metabolic wastes stored in dead cells, resins and gums, or shed with old leaves
waste products are stored in cellular vacuoles

reviewNotes: The scheme prints one total of 2 and lists four points under 'any two'; the 1+1 split is inferred, but it is the only split the scheme's own wording supports.

The opening rebuttal ('It is completely wrong to say that plants do not produce any excretory products') earns no separate mark, and after checking the scheme it stays that way: CBSE really is this harsh here. The only quantity the scheme prints is '(any two)', and it attaches to the four strategies, so on a 2-mark question the two marks are those two points at 1 each. Paying the rebuttal 1 mark would leave the strategies at ½ each and would drop a student who lists two strategies without an explicit rebuttal — the scheme's own model answer — from 2/2 to 1/2. That is a larger wrong than the one it would fix.
So a student who only rebuts and lists nothing scores zero, by the scheme. This rubric stays needsReview, which means no grader may paint that answer red until a teacher signs the reading off.

rubrics.subject: Science
rubrics.prompt: How many chambers are there in the heart of (i) fishes and (ii) humans? How is mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood prevented?

steps.awardFor: two chambers in a fish heart; blood is pumped to the gills, oxygenated, and passes directly to the body
four chambers in the human heart; the septum separates the right and left sides and prevents mixing

partial.note: chamber count right, no mechanism for preventing mixing

reviewNotes: The scheme prints one total of 2 for both sub-parts; the 1+1 split is inferred from the two numbered sub-parts.

rubrics.subject: Science
rubrics.prompt: Draw and explain how the nerve cells help in transmission of impulses.

scheme.excerpt: All information from our environment is detected by the specialised tips of some nerve cells. The information acquired at the end of the dendritic tip of a nerve cell (Fig. a), sets off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse. This impulse travels from the dendrite to the cell body, and then along the axon to its end. At the end of the axon, the electrical impulse sets off the release of some chemicals. These chemicals cross the gap, or synapse, and start a similar electrical impulse in a dendrite of the next neuron. This is how nervous impulses travel in the body. (Fig b). [3]

steps.awardFor: a correct labelled figure of a neuron showing the path an impulse takes through it
information is detected at the dendritic tip, setting off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse
the impulse travels to the cell body and along the axon, and at the axon's end chemicals are released that cross the synapse and start a similar impulse in the next neuron

partial.note: traces part of the path — the axon or the synapse is named, but the chain through to the next neuron is not completed

reviewNotes: The scheme prints one total of 3 for the whole answer and no per-step marks at all, so every split of it is inferred. This rubric reserves 1 for the figure and 2 for the explanation.

The figure mark is not printed by CBSE. It is reserved because the stem says 'Draw and explain' and because the scheme's own model answer cites (Fig. a) and (Fig b) inside its prose — the drawing is part of the answer CBSE describes. Without it a student who draws a correct labelled neuron and writes nothing scores zero, which is the worse error. A teacher who reads the scheme as 3 marks of prose should move this mark back into the explanation.

The explanation's three prose bullets are merged into two steps (impulse generation; conduction along the axon and transmission across the synapse) so that the two remaining marks are whole marks. The merge is this author's, not CBSE's.

rubrics.subject: Science
rubrics.prompt: Puneet wants to grow banana plants. (i) Should he opt for seeds or another method of reproduction? Justify. (ii) What causes variation, and are variations good or bad? Justify.

steps.awardFor: rejects seeds, because banana plants have lost the capacity to produce seeds

any: lost the capacity to produce seeds

steps.awardFor: recommends vegetative propagation, by stem cutting

partial.note: names vegetative propagation but no method

steps.awardFor: errors and variations in DNA copying cause variation
variation is good — it helps a population tide over unfavourable conditions through the survival of some variants
any one way variation can be bad

options.awardFor: the parents' desirable characters are lost
some variants cannot survive the new conditions
the variant cannot use the cellular apparatus efficiently

reviewNotes: The scheme prints one total of 5 across both sub-parts; the 2 + 3 split, and the 1+1 inside each, are inferred.

Sub-part (ii) is Heredity (jesc1 chapter 8) content sitting inside a reproduction question. Filed under chapter 7 because the question as a whole is about plant reproduction; a teacher may prefer chapter 8.

rubrics.subject: Science
rubrics.prompt: A pin is fixed to an aluminium wire with wax and the wire is heated. A. If the aluminium wire is replaced by silver, will the observation change? B. Will the aluminium wire melt?

steps.awardFor: the pin still drops but takes less time, because silver is a better conductor of heat than aluminium

partial.note: says the pin drops faster but gives no reason

steps.awardFor: no, the aluminium wire will not melt, because metals have high melting points

partial.note: answers 'no' with no reason

rubrics.subject: Science
rubrics.prompt: Sara neutralises dilute NaOH with dilute H2SO4 using phenolphthalein. A. Would concentrated acid need more or fewer than 40 drops? Justify. B. How many mL of NaOH did 3 mL of H2SO4 neutralise? OR, starting from 10 drops of acid, what colour change follows 20 drops of NaOH and why? C. Write the equation and classify the reaction.

scheme.excerpt:
28 A. (b) < 40, because concentrated H2SO4 gives more H+ ions than dilute acid. B. 3 mL of H2SO4 will be 60 drops, which will neutralise 6 mL of NaOH [table: 2 mL/20 drops (1 mL), 3 mL/30 drops (1.5 mL), 4 mL/40 drops (2 mL), 6 mL/3 mL = 60 drops]
OR
Colour will change from colourless to pink. Phenolphthalein in colourless in acids and turns pink in basic solution. C. 2NaOH + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2H2O (a) neutralisation and double displacement reaction. Base NaOH is getting neutralised and forming salt + water. It is double displacement as Na+ ions are being replaced by H+ and OH- by SO4 2-. It is not precipitation reaction because Na2SO4 is soluble in water. [4]

steps.awardFor: sub-part A — fewer than 40 drops, because concentrated H2SO4 gives more H+ ions than dilute acid
sub-part B — whichever of the two printed alternatives the student answered

alternatives.label: the volume calculation (printed first)
alternatives.awardFor: 3 mL of acid is 60 drops, which neutralises 6 mL of NaOH

steps.awardFor: 3 mL is 60 drops, which neutralises 6 mL of NaOH

partial.note: numbers right, no volume unit written
the 20-drops-per-mL ratio is used but mis-multiplied

alternatives.label: the OR — the colour change
alternatives.awardFor: the solution turns from colourless to pink, because phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base

steps.awardFor: colourless to pink, because phenolphthalein is colourless in an acid and pink in a base

partial.note: names the pink colour but gives no reason from phenolphthalein's behaviour in a base

steps.awardFor: sub-part C — writes the balanced equation 2NaOH + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2H2O

partial.note: the right reactants and products, but the equation is not balanced

steps.awardFor: sub-part C — picks (a), neutralisation and double displacement, and says why: a base forms salt and water, the ions are exchanged, and Na2SO4 is soluble so nothing precipitates

partial.note: names the reaction correctly but gives no reason for the naming

reviewNotes: The scheme prints only the total of 4; no sub-part carries a printed mark. The 1 (A) + 1 (B) + 2 (C) split is inferred from the paper's case-study convention, and the 1 + 1 inside C — equation, then classification with its justification — is inferred too. An earlier draft split C as ½ equation + ½ naming + 1 justification; that was changed because a ½-mark step admits no partial credit, so a right-but-unbalanced equation scored zero.

Sub-part B carries an OR inside it, with no 'attempt either' header of its own — the scheme simply prints OR between the volume calculation and the colour-change answer. Both branches are modelled as a kind: "alternatives" step, each worth the sub-part's whole 1 mark. Before this change a student who answered the OR scored zero.
Sub-part A's option letter (b) is not required by s1; the rubric asks for the value and the reason, which is what the scheme's own sentence gives.

rubrics.subject: Science
rubrics.prompt: A student needs a 0.12 Ω resistor from copper wire of 0.80 mm diameter (ρ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ωm). (i) Determine the cross-sectional area. (ii) Calculate the length required.

steps.awardFor: uses A = πd²/4 with d = 0.80 × 10⁻³ m to get approximately 5 × 10⁻⁷ m²

partial.note: area right, m² not written
the area formula is quoted and never substituted into

steps.awardFor: rearranges R = ρl/A to l = RA/ρ and gets approximately 3.33 m

partial.note: length right, m not written
the length is quoted before the area is established

reviewNotes: The scheme prints one total of 3 with no split; 1½ + 1½ is inferred from the two sub-parts.

rubrics.subject: Science
rubrics.prompt: (i) Is the student's claim that the magnetic field at X is stronger than at Y correct? Explain. (ii) Redraw the diagram and mark the direction of the field lines.

steps.awardFor: states that the closeness of the field lines is directly related to the strength of the field
concludes the field at X, at the pole, is stronger than at Y — the claim is correct

partial.note: agrees the claim is correct but does not tie it to the pole

steps.awardFor: redraws the diagram with arrows marked correctly from North to South

reviewNotes: The scheme prints one total of 3 and three prose bullets, one of which is the redraw instruction. The 1 + 1 + 1 split is the author's inference, not CBSE's — the scheme allots no per-step marks. Confirm the split before a grader is allowed to mark any of these steps wrong.
Sub-part (ii) is a redraw, so it is a diagram step and stays unmarked for a human. A student who redraws correctly and writes nothing therefore caps at 1 of 3 once signed off.

rubrics.subject: Mathematics
rubrics.prompt: The sum of the first n terms of an AP is 5n² − n. Find the nth term of the AP.

steps.awardFor: states the relation aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁

rubrics.subject: Social Science
rubrics.prompt: 'The Silk route was a good example of vibrant pre-modern trade and cultural links between distant parts of the world.' Explain with any two examples.

steps.awardFor: any two examples of trade or cultural exchange along the silk routes

options.awardFor: Chinese pottery, textiles and Indian spices travelled west; precious metals flowed from Europe to Asia
Buddhism spread from India in several directions through the intersecting points of the silk routes
early Christian missionaries and later Muslim preachers travelled this route to reach Asia

rubrics.subject: Social Science
rubrics.prompt: Rice is a commercial crop in Haryana and Punjab but a subsistence crop in Odisha. Explain why, using geographical factors and economic practices.

steps.awardFor: any two contrasts between the two regions

options.awardFor: Punjab and Haryana have well-developed canal irrigation and a climate suited to high-yielding varieties; Odisha's rice is largely rainfed
Punjab and Haryana grow rice for national and international markets with government procurement and transport; Odisha grows mostly for local use
Punjab and Haryana use modern machinery and high-yielding varieties; Odisha's farming is traditional and family-scale

reviewNotes: The scheme requires 'at least one related to climate and one economic'. The farming-practices point is tagged economic here so that it can partner the climate point; a teacher may consider it a third, untagged category, in which case an answer of points 2 and 3 would no longer be full marks.

rubrics.subject: Social Science
rubrics.prompt: Highlight any two key features of federalism.

steps.awardFor: any two features of federalism

options.awardFor: there are two or more levels or tiers of government
each tier governs the same citizens but has its own jurisdiction in legislation, taxation and administration
the jurisdictions of each tier are specified in the constitution, so each tier's authority is constitutionally guaranteed
the fundamental provisions cannot be unilaterally changed by one level of government

any: not changed by one level alone

options.awardFor: courts interpret the constitution and the highest court umpires disputes between levels
sources of revenue for each level are clearly specified, ensuring financial autonomy

rubrics.subject: Social Science
rubrics.prompt: Sri Lanka and Belgium source passage. 28.1 State any two demands of Tamils in Sri Lanka. 28.2 State the results of the Majoritarian Government in Sri Lanka. 28.3 Explain any two provisions of the Belgian model of power sharing.

steps.awardFor: any one demand of the Sri Lankan Tamils

options.awardFor: recognition of Tamil as an official language
regional autonomy
equality of opportunity in education and jobs

steps.awardFor: the majoritarian government created distrust between Tamils and Sinhalas, which led to civil war, deaths on both sides, and families fleeing as refugees

partial.note: names the distrust but not the civil war or its consequences

steps.awardFor: any two provisions of the Belgian model of power sharing

options.awardFor: equal numbers of Dutch- and French-speaking ministers in the central government, with some laws needing majorities from each linguistic group

any: Dutch and French ministers shall be equal

options.awardFor: many central powers were given to the state governments of the two regions, which are not subordinate to the centre
Brussels has a separate government in which Dutch and French have equal representation
a third community government, elected by each language community, has power over cultural, educational and language issues

reviewNotes: The paper says 28.1 asks for 'any two demands' but the scheme prints '(Any one to be considered)' and allots 1 mark. This rubric follows the scheme, not the paper. A student who lists exactly one demand is full marks here.

rubrics.subject: Social Science
rubrics.prompt: Explain the importance of public facilities for development.

steps.awardFor: any two public facilities, each explained

options.awardFor: healthcare and public health — reduces mortality, keeps the workforce productive
education and skill development — equal learning opportunity, literacy, innovation, growth
sanitation and clean water — prevents disease, raises life expectancy, cuts healthcare costs
infrastructure — roads, transport and energy connect markets and improve quality of life

reviewNotes: The scheme allots 1½ + 1½ = 3 for 'any two', so a facility named without explanation should not take the full 1½. There is no half-of-1½ award in CBSE's grain, so no partial rule is declared on the group; a named-but-unexplained facility currently scores full or nothing. A teacher should decide whether a 1-mark partial is fair here.

rubrics.subject: Social Science
rubrics.prompt: Explain any three factors that have enabled globalisation.

steps.awardFor: any three factors, each well explained

options.awardFor: the movement of goods and services between countries
information and communication technology
transportation technology
the movement of people between countries
liberalisation of foreign trade and foreign investment policy

reviewNotes: The scheme says 'any 3 well explained' but lists the five factors as bare phrases with no explanation of its own. The keyword sets here therefore test only that the factor is named, not that it is explained — this rubric is more generous than an examiner would be.

rubrics.subject: Social Science
rubrics.prompt: Privatisation can have both positive and negative effects on the economy. Support the statement with argument.

steps.awardFor: any five effects of privatisation

options.awardFor: increased efficiency and productivity
improved quality of services
reduced burden on the government
exclusion of public welfare, because profit becomes the only motive
loss of employment security
a wider gap between rich and poor, because basic facilities become inaccessible
lower government accountability

reviewNotes: The scheme says 'ANY 5 points... however, at least 2 positive and 2 negative effects must be included'. Modelled as chooseAtLeast 5 with requireTags positive 2, negative 2. The fifth point may come from either side, which is what the scheme implies but does not say.

Privatisation is filed here under jess2 chapter 2 (Sectors of the Indian Economy), where public and private sectors are compared. It is also touched on in chapter 4 (Globalisation); a teacher may prefer that filing.
